meta.name: description
meta.content: Focused programming exercises, useful test feedback, and approachable course administration for numerical methods and computational finance teaching.

div.h1: More time for the mathematical question.
div.p: Programming exercises connect a mathematical method to its behavior on a computer. The surrounding classroom tools should make that connection easier to explore.

div.h2: A small lab can teach a lot.
div.p: An exercise does not need to be a large software project. A numerical method, a small simulation, or a computational finance experiment can be enough to provoke useful questions: Does the implementation match the definition? Which cases fail? How does floating-point arithmetic affect the result?

finmath classroom supports this kind of focused practice. Learners start from an instructor's template, work in their own private GitHub repository, and receive feedback from Maven and JUnit. The next experiment is only another change and test run away.
div.h2: Feedback while the question is still fresh.
div.p: Tests provide a concrete observation to discuss. A passing check can confirm one part of an approach; a failure can point to a missing case or mistaken assumption. Weighted methods and whole-suite rubrics let an instructor choose how to structure that feedback.

The administration tools collect those results into a local history, including missing and unavailable feedback. They preserve the difference between a failed test and a result that was never received.

Students may explore with or without AI tools, according to the course's rules. An explanation or code suggestion is a starting point for investigation. Students still need to inspect the implementation, choose useful test cases, and explain why an answer is appropriate.
Quick feedback supports that conversation. It does not replace mathematical reasoning, a discussion with the instructor, or the course's assessment policy.

The service uses Java, Spring MVC, SQLite, and ordinary configuration files. It provides a browser flow for learners and command-line tools for instructors. Assignment repositories retain their own builds and Git histories.

Hosting the administration service gives a course control over its configuration and stored registration data. GitHub supplies repository hosting, sign-in, and Actions; a live installation still needs the corresponding GitHub setup and a maintained server.
A test result is a reason to investigate.
Change something. Observe the result. Explain what you learned.
GitHub Classroom was retired on August 28, 2026. This project offers a free, self-hosted alternative focused on registration, private assignment repositories, and test feedback.
Student workflows, build files, and reports are student-controlled. Submission capture and an isolated, trusted final grader remain future work.
A fictional quadratic-equation exercise illustrates the flow from acceptance to feedback.
